label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong, Friday, Dec. 11, 1925.

label: text
text:
H.E. the Governor is to be congratulated on the speech he made to the Elders of the New Territory. It exhibits his own personal feelings, demonstrates anew the course of British Administration, bound up as it is with justice and equity, and should appeal to the sound and fundamental commonsense of the Chinese people. We have it on good authority that the Chinese like to be spoken to gently, that they are amenable to reason and are quick to see the reason and goodness in anything put before them. A touch of firmness, we should imagine, is also not lost, upon them. In all that H.E. the Governor said to the Elders on Saturday, there is not a thing but which can be heartily approved. Compensation to dispossessed villagers who have enjoyed sanctuary and repose, and who have carried on their quiet agricultural pursuits, is justice to what may be called the 21st degree. They are being dispossessed in the interests of a far greater number, a number which includes a vast population of their own people; but that dispossession is to be made good in generous and unstinted manner. Justice can go no further. Forest fires and the acts of unfriendly pickets are miles asunder. But the Governor's remarks admit of no counter argument. They may not suit the militant "direct action" person; but of their commonsense the friendly will not dispute. H.E. the Governor has come to the Colony at perhaps the most difficult and vital in its long history. His determination to improve the Colony remains unchanged. This gesture of friendliness to the Elders of the New Territory, and to the greater numbers under their influence is in the true spirit which has made the British Empire what it is. This spirit must percolate even those whose actions have been inimical to the best interests of this Colony and to the great concourse of Chinese who live here in peace and security. That being so, time will prove their effectiveness, ushering in a newer, better and more prosperous regime. His Excellency's utterances should be taken to heart by the foreign community. They constitute both precept and example and as such are not to be ignored.
HEALTH MATTERS
Some time last year in the course of the debate is when the

label: text
text: health system of the Colony. It was pointed out that in spite of the fact that Hongkong is one of the biggest shipping ports in the world it had not a quarantine station. It was contended against this that the Colony had got along without one for some considerable period. But in stressing the case for the provision of a station to prevent possible very serious outbreaks, Unofficials referred to the introduction here some time previously of cholera cases from a ship when the patients had had to be housed in junk. The then Colonial Secretary waxed facetious in his reply and referred to the particular case quoted as when "some people from a neighbouring port were so careless as to contract cholera and had had to be put on lighters." There had been two deaths. That was the only time Hongkong had experienced any very pressing need for a quarantine station in 80 years, stated Sir Claud Severn, leaving it presumably to be assumed that it was unlikely such need would be experienced again for a similar period. The Government were at the time, he admitted, in negotiation for the erection of a very fine quarantine station, and it would appear now that this was the old site and buildings of Rennie's Mills at Junk Bay, alterations to which are now on the point of completion. The site, as Dr. Addison stated yesterday, is a suitable one and much to be preferred to that which some years ago the Government had in view at Laichikok, now the jail, but prior to that a group of huts—relics of the days when extensive organisation was in being for supervising the exportation of Chinese labour for the diamond fields of South Africa. In the station at Junk Bay, we learn, it will be possible to accommodate practically two thousand people, but it is extremely improbable that the full capacity will ever be required. The Station will be kept for deck passengers from boats on which small-pox or cholera have been contracted, the lack of system formerly obtaining being extremely dangerous owing to the impossibility of keeping in touch with that class of person once landing in Hongkong had been effected. This lack of system was inevitable in the circumstances, but now there is a fine station in existence an end may be put at once to a state of affairs of which the Colony, to say the least, had no reason to be proud. There is a certain amount of truth in arguments that have been advanced with regard to the difficulty of keeping out infectious persons owing to the thousand of people who land by junk or cross the border; but that is no reason why one means of inlet, that which it is possible to check by means of ship's lists, should not be superintended most carefully. Coming by steamer is the most general means of entry and it is surely up to the Colony's health authorities to do what they can, and not merely point to what can't be helped. Their hands will be considerably strengthened by this new station and it must be a relief to them, with cholera notified from a neighbouring port, to feel that they have at last an institution to cope with urgent needs, however great those needs may at any time become.

label: text
text: Sir Gershom Stewart, K.B.E., of Hoylake, the former Conservative M.P. for Wirral, has been presented with his portrait in oils, painted by Mr. F. T. Copnall, who has exhibited it at the Liverpool Autumn Exhibition. Lady Stewart received a beautiful jewelled watch. The gifts were subscribed to by over 800 of Sir Gershom Stewart's former constituents—both Conservative and Liberal. In the portrait Sir Gershom is seen in the uniform of a Deputy Lieutenant. The gifts were accompanied by a bound volume containing the names of the subscribers, and an address, read by the Chairman.

Hongkong University
A COMING has spiritual, if not CENTENARY, actual bonds with it,

label: text
text: University of London is preparing to celebrate its first centenary in the spring of 1927 should be of some interest. A hundred years ago a letter from the poet Thomas Campbell to Mr. Henry Brougham, afterwards Lord Brougham, published in the "Times," formed the starting-point in the movement out of which the University arose. It is now proposed to raise the very considerable sum of £500,000 in celebration of the event. This sum is to be devoted in part to certain building schemes and, for the rest, to the endowment of teaching.

label: paragraph_title
text: WHEN WINTER COMES.

label: text
text: Those authoritative people who, with grave mien, tell us

label: text
text: officially of the arrival of the first touch of cold, have announced it. We can almost see a solemn and sardonic joy in their manner as they say, "See, you have had your summer. Now is come the advance guard of the winter of your discontent."

label: text
text: Winters of discontent need have no place in our lives. In what are called the bleak months, if we have no bleak minds there need be no bleak houses.

label: text
text: The hireside is the intimate stimulant of confidences. It is the mother's confessor of the human heart. We can enjoy by its autumn glow the majesty of Shakespeare, the Wagner of literature. We can enjoy by its glow, thanks to progress, the majesty of Wagner, the Shakespeare of music. There is a special tonic pleasure, too, in a crisp keen day of December on the top of a tramcar, in a ricsha or the more opulent motor car or breathing the lone hill amid tints of autumn's ample painting.

label: text
text: When winter comes let it come. Its bark is worse than its bite in Hongkong!

CHINESE HUMOUR THREB TYPOAL STORIES.
In The Chinese Student, this official organ of the Edinburgh Chinese Stu. C. K. Soo tells

label: text
text:
I.—SELF-CONTRADICTION.
Once there lived a man who made his living by making spears and shields. To every one he recommended his spears as the sharpest on the market, against which shields would be worse than useless. With equal enthusiasm, however, he praised his shields, on which he declared, no spears in existence could make the least impression.
So one day a customer asked him, "If I use one of your invulnerable shields in a combat against spears of your own make, what do you think the result would be?"
The man could not answer.

label: text
text: While crossing a lake in great haste, a native of T'zu neeidentally let his sword drop into the water. Thereupon, he immediately marked the exact spot on the stern of the boat from which it had slipped—in the belief that he would be able to recover the lost weapon on arrival at the opposite shore by using the mark as a line!

label: text
text: One beautiful moonlight night is villager had occasion to draw water out of it well. On seeing the reflection of the moon in the water, he exclaimed, "My word, this is serious. The moon has fallen!" Without another thought he set himself to the heroic task of rescuing Cynthia in distress. He emptied one pill after another as fast as he could, but still to no purpose.

label: text
text: At length he became so exhausted that he fell on his back. As he now caught sight of the moon reigning in the firmament in all her splendour, he sighed with great relief, "I am indeed tired; but I have done good work!"

Washington, Dec. 10.
Foreign debts hitherto funded
total $7,390,000,000, and $4,743,000,000 remain unfunded, the major portion of which is French.
This is revealed by Mr. Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury, in his annual report.

label: text

Outlook, he asserted that the past year has been a period of genuine prosperity for practically all classes.
The present business situation warrants optimism for the future.
It is pointed out that though a tendency existed among the consuming public to buy every conceivable commodity on time and mortgage the future earnings, business people were conducting their affairs cautiously in order that prosperity would not bring carelessness.
He emphasised the intention to pursue a policy of economy.
The repayment of debts is recommended to the use of tax reduction which however should not be excessive.
